topics.title: Ram Mandir Fund Row
bullets: On 13 June 2026, the Uttar Pradesh government formed a three- member SIT to probe alleged embezzlement of donation funds at Ayodhya's Ram Temple.
The controversy erupted after Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav claimed on 7 June 2026 that crores of rupees from temple donations were missing.
The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust itself requested the probe, calling it a conspiracy to damage the temple's image. History –
In 1528, a mosque was built at the site by Mughal emperor Babar, which Hindus claim to be the birthplace of Lord Ram and where a temple existed earlier.
Between 1853 and 1949, communal violence occurred at the site periodically; the British administration gave the inner court for Muslims and the outer court for Hindus.
In 1855, a dispute arose when Sunni Muslims claimed that a temple in nearby Hanumangarh was built after demolishing a mosque, further entrenching the religious flashpoint.
In December 1949, an idol of Lord Ram was placed inside the Babri Masjid, prompting Muslims to protest; the government declared the premises a disputed area and locked the gates.
In 1950, two suits were filed in the Faizabad civil court for rights to perform pooja of Ram Lalla and keep the idols in the structure. Nirmohi Akhara filed a third suit in 1959.
In 1961, the UP Sunni Central Wakf Board filed a suit demanding possession of the site and removal of idols, adding a formal Muslim party to the litigation.
In 1986, a district judge ordered the locks to be removed and the site opened for Hindu worshippers, marking a significant turning point in the dispute.
The Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP) launched a movement to reclaim the land and birthplace of Lord Ram, with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) lending its support and making it a poll plank.
This period saw the transformation of the Ayodhya dispute from a local legal matter into a national political movement.
On 6 December 1992, the Babri Masjid was demolished by kar sevaks (volunteers) gathered at the site, an event that shocked the nation and the world.
The demolition triggered widespread Hindu-Muslim violence across the country, leaving more than 2,000 people dead.
The then Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, Kalyan Singh, resigned following the demolition, taking moral responsibility for the incident.
In 2001, a special judge dropped criminal conspiracy charges against 13 accused, including senior BJP leaders L.K. Advani and Kalyan Singh, a decision later challenged.
In 2010, the Allahabad High Court delivered a landmark verdict, awarding two-thirds of the disputed site to Hindu parties and one-third to the Sunni Waqf Board.
In 2011, the Supreme Court stayed the Allahabad High Court verdict, setting the stage for a final adjudication at the apex court level.
In 2017, the Supreme Court called for an out-of-court settlement and restored criminal conspiracy charges against top BJP leaders.
In March 2019, the apex court referred the land dispute case for mediation, asking the panel to complete proceedings within eight weeks; however, the mediation failed.
On 6 August 2019, the Supreme Court began day-to-day hearings, which continued for 40 days before concluding on 16 October 2019.

On 9 November 2019, a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court unanimously awarded the entire 2.77 acres of disputed land to the deity Ram Lalla, paving the way for the construction of a Ram temple.
The Court also directed the central government to allot an alternative five-acre plot to the Sunni Waqf Board for the construction of a mosque in Ayodhya.
The verdict brought a judicial closure to a dispute that had lingered for over a century, with the Court holding that the demolition of the mosque was illegal.
Following the Supreme Court verdict, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the formation of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust in the Lok Sabha on 5 February 2020.
The trust was set up to oversee and manage the construction of the Ram Mandir, composed of 15 trustees as directed by the Supreme Court.
The trust was awarded the disputed 2.77-acre land as well as an additional 67.703-acre land acquired under the Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993.
The central government nominated 12 of the 15 members of the trust, with K. Parasaran, the former Attorney General who represented Ram Lalla in the Ayodhya case, made acting chairman initially.
On 19 February 2020, the trust nominated its remaining members and elected Mahant Nrityagopal Das as chairman and Champat Rai as general secretary.
The trust has 15 members in total, comprising 9 permanent members and 6 nominated members, all of whom must be practicing Hindus.
In November 2020, the trust appointed Larsen & Toubro as the design and build contractor and Tata Consulting Engineers as the project manager for the temple's construction.
The trust also signed contracts for the development of the 67-acre temple complex, with the construction targeted for completion by August 2026.

The temple construction, undertaken by Engineers India Limited, has been progressing with multiple phases, including the main sanctum, parikrama paths and six newly built shrines. Structural and architectural details –
Built on 2.7 acres, the three-story Ram Mandir has a length of 380 feet (east-west), a width of 250 feet, and a height of 161 feet.
The intricately carved structure features 392 pillars, 44 doors, and stands at about 70% of the Qutub Minar's height.
Chief architect Chandrakant B Sompura designed it in the Nagara style, with five mandaps (pavilions) and five shikharas (spires) rising to 161 ft.
The Nagara style, known for its beehive or curvilinear tower, originated in North India during the late Gupta period (5th Century CE).
Key features include a sanctum (garbhagriha), a front hall (mandapa), and the signature curvilinear tower (shikhara) representing the mythical Mount Meru.
This style celebrates symmetry and is constructed entirely of stone, without using iron or steel, ensuring the temple stands for at least 1,000 years.
The foundation is built on a 1.5-meter-thick concrete raft, a 6.3- meter-thick granite plinth, and 47 layers of engineered soil reaching 15 meters deep.
The primary stone is Bansi Paharpur Pink Sandstone from Rajasthan, with white Makrana marble (from the Taj Mahal) adorning the sanctum sanctorum
The ground floor houses the Garbhagriha (sanctum sanctorum) with the idol of Ram Lalla, sculpted from Mysore black granite
The first floor features the Shri Ram Darbar, with King Ram, Sita, Lakshman, and Hanuman, carved from white Makrana marble.
Gold-plating adorns 14 doors, including the main entrance, and six special Makrana marble pillars feature carvings of over 10,000 idols.
The temple complex features five distinct mandaps (pavilions): Nritya Mandap (Dance), Rang Mandap (Color), Gudh Mandap (Assembly), Kirtan Mandap (Devotional Song), and Prarthana Mandap (Prayer).
The mandaps are supported by 160 columns on the ground floor and 132 columns on the first floor.
The primary main shikhara is 128 feet tall and the other two shikharas are 76 feet tall
The main temple is surrounded by the Parkota, a 732-meter-long rectangular compound wall that is 14 feet thick.
At the four corners of the Parkota are temples for Surya (Sun), Bhagwati, Ganesh, and Shiv.

The northern arm has a Maa Annapurna temple, the southern arm a Hanuman temple, and ancient temples on the upper floor include Maharshi Valmiki, Vashishtha, Vishwamitra, Agastya, Nishad Raj, Mata Shabri, and Devi Ahilya.
The project used traditional Indian construction technology; the intricate stone carvings were done by approximately 1,500 skilled artisans.
The temple complex is designed to be eco-friendly, with 70% of the 70-acre area left as green space.
At an estimated cost of ₹1,800 crore, the project was designed by the Sompura family and built by Larsen & Toubro (L&T).
A Pilgrims Facility Centre (PFC) with a capacity of 25,000 people is available, along with ramps and lifts for the elderly and differently-abled.
The temple is built to withstand earthquakes and is declared completely safe for at least 2,500 years.
The complex also features a sewage treatment plant, an independent power station, and a water treatment plant. Pran Pratishtha –

On 22 January 2024, the idol of Ram Lalla was consecrated in the main sanctum (garbhagriha) of the Ram Mandir in a grand pran pratishtha ceremony. Prime Minister Modi led the rituals as the master of ceremony.
The ceremony marked the formal opening of the temple to devotees after centuries of legal and political battles.
In the first 11 days after inauguration, the temple reportedly received around Rs 11 crore in donations, averaging nearly Rs 1 crore per day.
In June 2025, the installation of the Ram Darbar — featuring idols of Ram, Sita, Lakshman and Hanuman — was completed, marking a second round of consecration activities.
This event was seen as another milestone in the temple's completion, with many devotees treating it as a significant spiritual moment.
The occasion was known as 'Pratishtha Dwadashi' and was celebrated on 11 January 2025, exactly one year after the main consecration.
On 25 November 2025, Prime Minister Modi hoisted the saffron Dhwaja (flag) atop the 161-foot spire of the Ram Mandir, an event many devotees described as a symbolic "second pran pratishtha".
The ceremony, scheduled on Vivah Panchami (the day marking the divine wedding of Lord Ram and Goddess Sita), was seen as the formal declaration of the temple's completion.
Trust general secretary Champat Rai announced that all construction work on the Ram Mandir was now complete, including the main sanctum, parikrama paths and six newly built shrines.
Since its consecration on 22 January 2024, the Ram Mandir has registered over 15 crore devotees and received donations exceeding Rs 500 crore as of June 2026.
Of this, around Rs 150 crore was collected from donation boxes, while the remaining Rs 350 crore was received via online channels and counters.

The temple currently receives donations of Rs 8 to 10 lakh daily at its donation boxes and counters, with six large donation boxes installed and a dozen more at other temples within the complex. Recent News –

On 7 June 2026, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav posted on X, citing reports that crores of rupees donated to the Ram Temple were missing, terming the matter "extremely sensitive" for devotees of Lord Ram.
He demanded that the judiciary take suo motu cognisance of the issue and questioned the silence of both the temple trust and the state government.
He described the situation as "utterly shameful" for the temple trust, stating that no one was coming forward to offer any explanation.
On the same day, former Samajwadi Party minister Pawan Pandey, who is the former MLA from Ayodhya, alleged that between Rs 5 crore and Rs 7.5 crore had been stolen from the temple's donation boxes.
Pandey called for a thorough investigation into the matter, raising the first concrete figure regarding the alleged misappropriation.
These allegations formed the immediate trigger for the controversy that would soon engulf the temple trust and the state government.
Trust general secretary Champat Rai said the ongoing internal audit had not revealed any major discrepancies.
He noted that the audit process continues and nothing notable has emerged so far.
However, a Trust member told Hindustan Times that only an impartial SIT probe could bring justice, as a trust-led probe would face questions.
As the controversy deepened, police recovered Rs 10-12 lakh from the residence of a temple employee in Ayodhya's Rudauli, who was involved in the counting of cash donations.
The raid was conducted at the residence of Lavkush Mishra, who worked in temple administration. Prior to this job, he worked as a car mechanic.
This recovery added urgency to the matter and prompted the state government to take decisive action.
Based on information provided by five employees associated with donation counting, around Rs 2 crore has been recovered so far from multiple individuals.
The five individuals – Lavkush, Avneesh, Anukalp, Karune and Ramashankar – have reportedly confessed to their involvement in the theft.
Two of them, Lavkush and Anukalp, are currently in police custody as investigations continue.
Donation boxes are placed at 14 locations in the Ram Temple complex, with cash taken to a highly secure "confidential room" for counting, the exact location kept secret for security.

A total of 50 personnel were involved in the counting process: 24 note-counting staff (employed through a private agency), 12 Trust employees (for supervision), and 14 officials and auditors from SBI and TCS.
Most employees hired through the private agency reportedly earn a monthly salary of around Rs 14,500, making their sudden wealth particularly suspicious.

On 13 June 2026, the Uttar Pradesh government announced the formation of a three-member Special Investigation Team (SIT) to probe the allegations, acting on the request of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust.
The SIT comprises Lucknow Divisional Commissioner Vijay Vishwas Pant, Inspector General of Police (Lucknow range) Kiran S, and Special Secretary (Finance) Neel Ratan.
The team has been directed to submit a preliminary report within seven days and a final report within 15 days.

topics.title: Gallantry Awards
bullets: President Droupadi Murmu honoured 51 brave personnel at Phase-I of the Defence Investiture Ceremony 2026 held at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
The awards included 7 Kirti Chakras, 15 Vir Chakras, and 29 Shaurya Chakras for acts of raw courage and total disregard for personal safety.
Among the awardees was Gaganyaan astronaut-designate Group Captain (now Air Commodore) Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair, who received a Kirti Chakra. What are Gallantry Awards? –
Gallantry Awards are among India's highest honours, conferred on military personnel and civilians for exceptional bravery, courage, and self-sacrifice in service to the nation.
They are presented by the President of India, who is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces.
The awards are announced twice a year, first on Republic Day (26 January) and then on Independence Day (15 August).
Wartime awards recognise acts of conspicuous gallantry in the presence of the enemy, such as during wars or battles.

Peacetime awards are for acts of bravery, valor, or self-sacrifice in the face of the enemy, such as during counter-insurgency operations, rescue missions, disaster response, and internal security duties.
These two categories reflect the different operational contexts in which India's security forces demonstrate unparalleled courage. History –
On 26 January 1950, India instituted its first three wartime gallantry awards: the Param Vir Chakra (PVC), the Maha Vir Chakra (MVC), and the Vir Chakra (VrC).
The Param Vir Chakra is India's highest military decoration for the most conspicuous bravery in the presence of the enemy.
The Maha Vir Chakra is the second-highest, and the Vir Chakra is the third-highest wartime gallantry award in India.
In 1952, India introduced three peacetime gallantry awards, initially called Ashoka Chakra Class-I, Class-II, and Class-III, made retroactive to 15 August 1947.
In January 1967, these decorations were officially renamed the Ashoka Chakra, the Kirti Chakra, and the Shaurya Chakra respectively.
This renaming aligned the peacetime awards with the wartime Chakra series.
Over time, several other gallantry decorations have been instituted for specific situations and services.
The Sena Medal (Gallantry) was established in 1960 for gallantry by Indian Army personnel not in the face of the enemy.
The Nau Sena Medal (Gallantry) and Vayu Sena Medal (Gallantry) were similarly established for the Navy and Air Force.
The Param Vir Chakra is a circular bronze disc, featuring four replicas of Indra's Vajra around the State Emblem on the obverse.
The ribbon is plain purple. A recipient is entitled to use the post-nominal letters "PVC".
So far, the Param Vir Chakra has been awarded only 21 times, of which 14 were posthumous awards.
The Maha Vir Chakra is the second-highest wartime gallantry award, conferred for conspicuous gallantry in the presence of the enemy.
The medal is made of standard silver, featuring a five-pointed heraldic star with a gold-gilt centre.
Its ribbon is half white and half orange. The post-nominal letters are "MVC".
The Vir Chakra is India’s third-highest gallantry award, presented for acts of gallantry in the presence of the enemy on land, sea, or air.
It is a standard silver medal with a five-pointed heraldic star and gold-gilt centre.
The ribbon is half blue and half orange. The post-nominal letters are "VrC". A total of 1322 Vir Chakra Awards have been awarded to date, with 361 awarded posthumously.
The Ashoka Chakra is India's highest peacetime gallantry award, equivalent to the Param Vir Chakra for peacetime acts of bravery.
It is a gold-gilt medal featuring the Ashoka Chakra surrounded by a lotus wreath.
The ribbon is green, divided by one orange vertical line. Post-nominal letters are "AC".
The Kirti Chakra is the second-highest peacetime gallantry award, conferred for conspicuous gallantry other than in the face of the enemy.
It is a standard silver medal with the Ashoka Chakra surrounded by a lotus wreath.
Its ribbon is green, divided into three equal parts by two orange vertical lines, with the post-nominal letters "KC".
The Shaurya Chakra is the third-highest peacetime gallantry award, recognising acts of gallantry other than in the face of the enemy.
It is a bronze medal featuring the Ashoka Chakra surrounded by a lotus wreath.
The ribbon is green, divided into four equal parts by three orange vertical lines, with the post-nominal letters "SC".
Article 18(1) of the Constitution of India abolishes titles and prohibits the state from conferring any titles, except military and academic distinctions.
In the landmark case Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1995), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of National Awards.
The Court clarified that National Awards do not amount to "titles" within the meaning of Article 18(1) and that they should not be used as suffixes or prefixes.
While the Supreme Court has prohibited using national award names as suffixes or prefixes, this prohibition does not apply to gallantry awards.
Gallantry awards such as the Param Vir Chakra, Ashoka Chakra, and Kirti Chakra can be legitimately used as prefixes (e.g., PVC Rajkumar Singh).
This distinction is crucial for understanding the constitutional position of gallantry decorations in India's legal framework. Eligibility –

For the wartime awards (PVC, MVC, VrC), all ranks of the Naval, Military, Air, Reserve, and Territorial Forces, including medical, nursing, and civilian staff serving under their direction, are eligible.

For the peacetime awards, all ranks of the Armed Forces, Reserve and Territorial Forces, Nursing Services, Police, Central Para-Military Forces, Railway Protection Force (RPF), and civilian citizens are eligible. Recent News –
On 8 June 2026, President Droupadi Murmu presented 51 gallantry awards at Phase-I of the Defence Investiture Ceremony 2026 held at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
These awards were given for exceptional acts of bravery by personnel of the Armed Forces, Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), and State and Union Territory Police.
The President conferred 7 Kirti Chakras (including 2 posthumous), 15 Vir Chakras (including 3 posthumous), and 29 Shaurya Chakras (including 1 posthumous) - Total – 51.
Group Captain (now Air Commodore) Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair, call sign “Papa”, was among the Kirti Chakra awardees for his distinguished service as a Gaganyaan astronaut-designate.
He is one of the four selected Gagannauts for India’s first human spaceflight mission, Gaganyaan.

Six bravehearts were awarded posthumous gallantry honours at the Defence Investiture Ceremony 2026. Passage: In 2026, India added its 100th wetland to the list of Ramsar Sites, marking a significant milestone in the country's conservation efforts. Ramsar Sites are wetlands designated under the Ramsar Convention, an international treaty aimed at promoting the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands. The recognition reflects the ecological importance of wetlands in maintaining biodiversity, regulating water cycles, supporting livelihoods, and mitigating climate-related risks. India has witnessed a rapid increase in the number of Ramsar Sites over the past decade, with wetlands ranging from high-altitude lakes and riverine ecosystems to coastal lagoons and mangrove habitats receiving international recognition. Wetlands are often described as among the world's most productive ecosystems and provide critical habitat for migratory birds, aquatic species, and endangered wildlife. Source: The Hindu The Ramsar Convention was adopted in: A. 1965 B. 1968 C. 1971 D. 1975
